how-much-to-charge-to-replace-a-furnace..text:
← Furnace bid calculator

How much to charge to replace a furnace

The number a homeowner wants is a published “$2,495 installed” furnace special, or a price they saw for a basement swap on a coupon site. That number is not a takeoff. A 60k 80% AFUE hang with fifteen included feet of duct is not the same job as a 100k 96% condensing unit in an attic with a matching coil, a gas upsize, forty feet of duct, haul-away of the old unit, and a new thermostat. The trip is the same. The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count the attic and the coil, not just the swap

HVAC-maintenance calculators price a recurring service contract. Mini-split calculators price ductless heads and a line-set. Water-heater calculators price a vent, a gas upsize, and an attic for a water heater. A furnace job is a changeout: the unit, where it sits, the coil, the gas, and the duct that is not in the coupon. Quoting all of that from a published special is how the first attic condensate run eats the field margin.

A job with the same trip can cost much more

Each extra foot past the included run is time that never appears on the coupon. An attic set is billed as its own hours. A matching coil, a gas upsize, haul-away, and a thermostat are adders that get forgotten on a brochure special. On the sample rates a 100k 96% condensing unit with a matching coil, a gas upsize, 40 feet of duct, haul-away, and a thermostat prices about $10,940.47 ($273.51 per foot of duct, 17.1 crew-hours). The same shop’s 60k 80% basement swap prices about $4,013.20 ($334.43 per foot, 5.8 hours, walk-away $2,608.58). Matching the brochure job’s $2,495 special on the attic-and-coil house is how that job becomes a loss — the walk-away on the heavy job is already $7,111.30, and the $2,495 special loses $113.58 even on the brochure basement swap.

A heat-pump attic set is not automatically the cheap one

An 80k heat pump with a matching coil, haul-away, and a thermostat in an attic is not the 60k 80% special minus 100%. On the sample rates that heat-pump job prices about $11,474.41 ($382.48 per foot, 15.2 crew-hours) — more than the brochure swap, not because the outdoor unit is slower but because attic hours, a coil, and a $1,600 equipment premium do not live in a published basement special. An 80k 96% basement unit with 25 feet of duct and haul-away prices about $6,260.60 (8.9 hours). Treating either as a blended add-on is how the special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first condensate run.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $52/h tech loaded at 34% payroll burden is $69.68. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not an HVAC design, a Manual J load calculation, a building-code determination, a permit, an engineering stamp, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Capacity, AFUE or HSPF, location, coil match, gas, and duct are yours to confirm.

Price your furnace job

Common questions

How much to charge to replace a furnace?

Charge from the trip, the set, extra duct past the included run, attic versus basement, BTU capacity, 80% versus 96% versus heat pump, a matching coil, a gas upsize, haul-away, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 60k 80% AFUE basement swap that stays inside the included footage, at the sample rates in this calculator, prices around $4,013 — about $334 per foot of duct.

Why is a $2,495 furnace special dangerous?

Homeowners count the swap. Extra duct, an attic set, a matching coil, a gas upsize, haul-away of the old unit, and a thermostat do not scale with that number. Matching a cheaper special written for a 60k 80% basement swap is how a 100k 96% attic-and-coil job becomes a two-day loss.

How much to charge to replace a furnace and matching coil in an attic?

An attic coil-and-gas job is not a basement-only special. On the sample rates a 100k 96% condensing unit with a matching coil, a gas upsize, 40 feet of duct, haul-away, and a thermostat prices around $10,940 ($274 per foot, 17.1 crew-hours), while a 60k 80% basement swap prices around $4,013 ($334 per foot, 5.8 hours).

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not HVAC, construction, legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice. You are responsible for verifying every figure before you rely on it or send a bid.

FOR HVAC SHOPS

Bid the attic, the coil, and the gas.

Price a furnace or heat-pump replacement the way the trade actually loses money: extra duct past the included run, attic versus basement, a matching coil, a gas upsize, haul-away of the old unit, and a thermostat. You get the bid, the price per foot of duct, and the walk-away number below which the job loses money.

The house

Start from a common job, then replace every figure with your takeoff. Changing capacity, equipment, or location never overwrites a rate you already typed.

Your crew rates

A $52/h tech loaded at 34% is $69.68. Quoting the raw wage on a published $2,495 installed special is how a 100k attic-and-coil changeout that looked fine turns into a two-day loss after the first condensate run.

Hand the customer a proposal

The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

Where the hours go

    Where the cost goes

      Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Starting hours and material rates are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a Manual J, or an HVAC design — replace them with your own takeoff.

      Common questions

      How can a competitor advertise a furnace replacement for $2,495?

      Usually because the special is written around one specific job: a 60,000 BTU 80% AFUE unit dropped into an open basement, with the first 15 ft of duct included, no coil, no gas work, no haul-away, and no thermostat. That job is one of the presets here, and it does price low. What does not scale with a trip charge is everything the coupon leaves out. Price your actual job beside it and the gap stops being a mystery and starts being a list of line items you can show the homeowner.

      Why is "included duct" its own field?

      Because that is where the coupon and the real job diverge. Only footage past the included run is charged — extra feet = max(0, duct run − included) — and those feet cost both material per foot and hours per foot. A 40 ft run against a 15 ft allowance is 25 ft of chargeable duct; a 12 ft basement run against the same allowance is zero, not a credit. That asymmetry is exactly what makes the brochure price honest on the small job and catastrophic on the big one.

      Why does the attic cost more than the basement for the same furnace?

      Access hours. A basement or open utility set is the baseline at zero extra hours, an interior closet adds about 1, and an attic adds about 2 — the carry, the platform, the working room, and the condensate run you cannot reach standing up. That is separate from the equipment premium: a 96% condensing furnace starts around 5.25 h to hang against 4 for an 80%, plus roughly $400 of material, and a heat pump around 6 h plus roughly $1,600. Attic + condensing stacks both.

      What does the calculator not include?

      It is not a Manual J, a load calculation, or an HVAC design, and picking 100,000 BTU here is not a finding that the house needs it — sizing is your load calc, not this page's. It also does not price recurring maintenance contracts, ductless mini-split installs, water-heater replacement, or standby generators; those are different jobs with their own tools. This prices a furnace or heat-pump changeout: the unit, where it sits, the coil, the gas, and the duct that is not in the coupon.

      Why isn't a 20% margin the same as adding 20% to my cost?

      Margin here is a share of the final price — price = total cost ÷ (1 − margin) — which is how the homeowner's number reads and how your books read it. Overhead is a separate markup on direct cost (labor + material + travel and equipment), applied before margin and never to itself or to profit. Marking a $6,000 cost up 20% gives $7,200, which is only a 16.7% margin; a 20% target margin gives $7,500. Across a heating season that gap is several installs.

      Is my pricing data uploaded anywhere?

      No. No account and no network requests — every wage, material cost, and price stays in this browser. A share link encodes only the inputs you choose into the address bar and is never sent to us. The business details saved for the printed proposal live in this browser's local storage, and "Forget my business details" clears them. The optional local usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your costs or prices, and the footer checkbox turns it off.

      No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not HVAC, construction, legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Usage counts are anonymous tallies of which features were used, stored locally, and never include your footage, wages, costs, or prices.

vs-a-flat-2495-furnace-special.html.text:
← Furnace / Heat Pump Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $2,495 furnace special

“$2,495 installed” is not a price for a furnace changeout — it is a price for one specific 60k basement swap, quietly applied to every furnace call that comes in.

What a flat $2,495 furnace special is

A flat installed price is the fastest number a shop can put on a postcard, a search ad, or a truck wrap: one price, no takeoff, easy for a homeowner to compare between bids. It works as a lead magnet, and it works for the homeowner as a round number to shop other companies against. Nothing about the number says which furnace, which location, or which extras it was built for.

The number was set for one job — commonly a smaller 60,000 BTU 80% AFUE furnace, swapped in an accessible basement with no more than the first 15 ft of duct, no matching coil, no gas upsize, no haul-away, and no new thermostat — and then quoted to every caller afterward, whether or not the next furnace looks anything like the one the special was priced on.

What this calculator does instead

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter capacity, equipment type (80% AFUE, 96% condensing, or heat pump), and location (basement, closet, or attic), with duct footage past the included run, a matching coil, a gas upsize, haul-away of the old unit, and a thermostat as their own line items, plus your crew's loaded wage, travel and equipment, overhead, and target margin. It turns that into the price, the effective hourly rate, and a walk-away price below which the job loses money — for this furnace, not the furnace the special was built on.

What a flat $2,495 special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same price whether the job is a 60,000 BTU basement swap with 15 ft of duct or a 100,000 BTU attic changeout with 40 ft of duct, a matching coil, and a gas upsize. Prices extra duct footage, capacity, and location as their own hour and material lines, so a bigger, harder job returns a bigger number instead of the same one.
Has no line for a matching coil, a gas upsize, haul-away of the old unit, or a new thermostat — a fully-loaded attic changeout prices the same as a bare basement swap. Adds coil hours and material, gas-upsize hours and fittings, haul-away hours and fee, and thermostat hours and cost only when that scope is turned on, so a loaded job shows up in the price instead of being absorbed into it.
Was priced once, on one furnace, and never re-derived from capacity, location, or extras — it is a marketing number, not a cost-basis number. Recomputes crew hours and materials from the exact capacity, location, and extras entered every time, so the price tracks the job rather than a memory of the postcard rate.
On this calculator's own 60k basement-swap preset — the exact job the $2,495 number is named for — the flat special already sits $113.58 below that job's own walk-away cost, before a dollar of profit. Returns a walk-away price of $2,608.58 and a bid price of $4,013.20 for that same basement swap, at this tool's own shop-rate defaults and a 35% target margin.
Gives the crew a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price, the price per extra duct foot, and the effective hourly rate, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the crew commits to it.

Two changeouts, the same capacity-blind rate

Using this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates ($52/hr crew wage, 34% burden, $155 travel and equipment, 18% overhead, a 35% target margin):

JobThis calculator's priceA flat $2,495 specialGap
60k 80% AFUE basement swap, first 15 ft of duct included — the job the flat number is named for$4,013.20 bid price; $2,608.58 break-even cost$2,495.00The flat special runs $113.58 under this job's own break-even cost, before a dollar of profit, and $1,518.20 under the calculator's own bid price — even on the exact job it claims to price.
100k 96% condensing, attic, matching coil, gas upsize, 40 ft duct, haul-away, thermostat$10,940.47 bid price; $7,111.30 break-even cost$2,495.00The same $2,495 special quotes $4,616.30 below this job's own break-even cost, and $8,445.47 below the calculator's bid price.

Both flat-rate rows use the literal $2,495 figure named in the calculator's own worked preset, applied to each job as a flat installed price regardless of capacity, location, or extras. Even the smallest, cheapest job the number is named for already loses money before profit is counted; a bigger changeout turns the same number into a five-figure loss. Run your own job's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat special is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one furnace it was built on, and nothing about a postcard rate tells a shop or a homeowner when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat special skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat $2,495 furnace special get a changeout wrong?

Because the cost driver is capacity, location, and extras, not "a furnace" alone. A 60,000 BTU 80% AFUE basement swap with its first 15 ft of duct included needs a fraction of the labor and material that a 100,000 BTU 96% condensing changeout in an attic needs, with a matching coil, a gas upsize, 40 ft of duct, haul-away of the old unit, and a new thermostat -- none of which scale with a flat installed price. A $2,495 special charges both the same.

What job is the $2,495 number actually built around?

One specific job: a smaller 60,000 BTU 80% AFUE furnace, swapped in an accessible basement or open utility space, with no more than the first 15 ft of duct, no matching coil, no gas upsize, no haul-away, and no new thermostat. It is a marketing price meant to get the phone to ring, not a number derived from any particular home's capacity, location, or extras.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates ($52/hr crew wage, 34% burden, $155 travel and equipment, 18% overhead, a 35% target margin): even the 60k basement swap the $2,495 number is named for has a walk-away cost of $2,608.58 and a bid price of $4,013.20 -- the flat special already sits $113.58 below that job's own break-even cost, before a dollar of profit, and $1,518.20 below the calculator's own bid price. Applied to a 100k 96% condensing changeout in an attic with a matching coil, a gas upsize, 40 ft of duct, haul-away, and a thermostat, the same $2,495 special is $4,616.30 below that job's own $7,111.30 walk-away cost, and $8,445.47 below the calculator's own bid price.

Is a flat furnace special ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of jobs close to the one the special was built around -- similar capacity, basement or open-utility access, no coil, no gas upsize, no haul-away -- a flat number can land close, though on this calculator's own worked example even that job already runs slightly under cost. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because the postcard price does not know which band a given job is in and neither does the crew until capacity, location, and extras are actually spelled out.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local labor or equipment rates. It takes the capacity, equipment type, location, duct footage, coil, gas upsize, haul-away, thermostat, and your own crew wage, burden, and overhead, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat special skips, not a market survey.

Open the Furnace / Heat Pump Bid Calculator to price your own job, or read the pricing walkthrough for how the math behind it works.

← Furnace / Heat Pump Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. ServiceTitan

Two different shapes: ServiceTitan is an account-based field service management platform for running an HVAC company's whole operation. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one furnace or heat-pump changeout cost, given its capacity, location, and extras, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

ServiceTitan is a field service management platform, founded in 2007 by Ara Mahdessian and Vahe Kuzoyan, headquartered in Glendale, California. It serves HVAC, electrical, plumbing, and other trades with scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, marketing, reporting, and job costing across a whole business, with a mobile app for crews in the field. It is an account-based platform: you sign up and use it as an ongoing service across a whole company, not a one-off calculator. ServiceTitan's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — field service management software serving the HVAC trade among others, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for ServiceTitan appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what ServiceTitan does. It does not schedule technicians, dispatch crews, or invoice a customer, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one job's capacity, equipment (80% AFUE, 96% condensing, or heat pump), and location (basement, closet, or attic), with duct footage past the included run, a matching coil, a gas upsize, haul-away of the old unit, and a thermostat as their own line items, plus loaded crew wage, payroll burden, travel and equipment, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the price, the price per duct foot and per extra duct foot, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a single printable customer proposal for that one job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Most HVAC shops get different value from each: ServiceTitan (or a comparable field service platform) for scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, and job costing across a whole company as an ongoing subscription, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to what one furnace or heat-pump changeout should cost from its capacity, location, and extras before a business system is involved. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a scheduled job, an invoice, or a signed proposal.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or ServiceTitan?

They do different jobs, and an HVAC shop of any size will likely end up touching both eventually. ServiceTitan is a field service management platform, founded in 2007 by Ara Mahdessian and Vahe Kuzoyan and headquartered in Glendale, California, used by HVAC, electrical, plumbing, and other trades to run scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, marketing, and reporting across a business, sold as an ongoing subscription account. This calculator does one narrower thing: starting from capacity, equipment, and location, with duct footage past the included run, a matching coil, a gas upsize, haul-away of the old unit, and a thermostat as their own line items, plus loaded crew cost, materials, overhead, and target margin, it turns that into the price, the price per extra duct foot, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money, before any of it touches a business-management system. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
